rv.q: Beane takes pinpoint aim, the jokes ricocheting across the commandeered basketball court
This musical about cheerleaders who withhold sex until their basketball team starts winning is surprisingly sweet and funny, with a terrific cast led by Patti Murin.

The joy of Lysistrata Jones is that it’s a pleasantly, peppily, so-dumb-it's-almost-clever undergraduate burlesque that's somehow made it to Broadway; the awkwardness of Lysistrata Jones is that it’s an undergraduate burlesque that's somehow made it to Broadway.
While no theatrical air ball, 'Lysistrata Jones' isn't a slam dunk, either.
Despite the ambitious concept and sporadic flashes of wit, Lysistrata Jones never quite finds its groove.
The plot remains silly, the music humdrum and the characters trite.
The show has energy and good intentions, but the forced merger of Aristophanes' ancient Greek comedy with contemporary basketball culture never quite gels into a satisfying theatrical experience.
The derivative combines campy comedic antics with no stakes whatsoever, unless some joker has given you Athens U. in the March Madness pool.

Don't get me started. I missed the upbeat show with the repugnant concept last summer when the Transport Group had a successful run with it downtown in a hip church gym. Transferred now to Broadway, the thing proves to be as trivializing and demeaning as it sounded.
Apart from a few new jokes and some heightened production values, 'Lysistrata Jones' remains unchanged and is as sharp and sassy as ever.
But too much of the time, it plays like a slightly raunchier version of a Nickelodeon or Disney Channel sitcom, rife with predictable plotlines and broad cultural and racial stereotypes.
Beane's book is the standout creative element, allowing the cast to deliver laughs you don't hate yourself for the next morning.
You can't combine so many cliches together and come up with something fresh.
Beane is the author of such amusing, sophisticated comedies as 'The Little Dog Laughed' and 'As Bees in Honey Drown,' as well as the very funny book for the musical 'Sister Act.
Junk food at Broadway prices is a tough sell.
The quality was really high in such an unusual place. But the show is now wilting under the white lights of Broadway and the air is seeping out of the ball.
